paragraphs.text: Security assessment is often treated as a separate activity from software development. Developers may receive vulnerability reports that identify a problem but provide little context about the affected code, its potential impact, or the steps needed to address it. Compliance requirements add another challenge, particularly when technical findings must be connected to documented controls or browser-extension store policies. These gaps make security review difficult to interpret and act upon, especially for small development teams.

paragraphs.text: This thesis presents ThreatLens, a web-based platform that brings codebase auditing, threat modeling, compliance assessment, and remediation guidance into a single workflow. Users can submit project archives for analysis and examine saved results through a read-only, editor-style workbench. The platform combines static security checks with language-model-assisted analysis to identify potential weaknesses and provide explanations grounded in available source evidence. Findings include severity, recorded file locations, relevant code excerpts, and remediation guidance.

paragraphs.text: The workbench connects source files with findings, control mappings, and suggested verification steps. An evidence-based graph helps users explore relationships between findings and affected components without presenting those relationships as confirmed exploitation paths. Security Advisor provides contextual explanations and code suggestions, while keeping proposed changes separate from the uploaded source. Browser-extension reviews extend this workflow to Chrome Web Store and Microsoft Edge Add-ons policies, distinguishing detected violations from requirements that need manual review or cannot be assessed from the submitted package.

paragraphs.text: ThreatLens also provides saved audit history, finding triage, comparison of compatible extension reviews, and downloadable reports. Workspace authorization, private source storage, evidence redaction, and time-limited source previews support controlled access to sensitive project information. Verification covers automated regressions, access-control checks, report generation, and representative browser workflows; these checks establish functional behavior rather than proving universal vulnerability-detection accuracy.

paragraphs.text: Software applications manage personal information, business transactions, communication and access to essential services. Their security depends partly on decisions made during development, including how inputs are validated, database queries are constructed, permissions are enforced and sensitive information is stored. A weakness in these areas can expose information or allow unintended operations. Security assessment must therefore form part of software development rather than being treated only as a final check before deployment. The Secure Software Development Framework published by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) supports integrating security practices throughout the software development life cycle. [1]

paragraphs.text: Reviewing source code becomes more demanding as projects grow across multiple files, frameworks and dependencies. A developer investigating a warning may need to locate the affected statement, understand the surrounding code and determine whether the reported condition is relevant to the application. Finding a potentially unsafe operation is only one part of this process. The reviewer must also decide what evidence supports the finding and how a proposed correction can be checked without changing the intended behaviour.

paragraphs.text: Static Application Security Testing helps identify suspicious code patterns without running the application. It provides a useful starting point for reviewing concerns such as injection, unsafe output handling and exposed credentials. However, a reported pattern is not necessarily an exploitable vulnerability. Static analysis can produce false positives and may miss problems that depend on runtime conditions, application state or business logic. Its results therefore require interpretation and verification. [2]

paragraphs.text: Language models offer another form of assistance by explaining code and suggesting possible remedies. These capabilities are useful when a finding is technically correct but difficult for a developer to understand. Nevertheless, generated explanations can contain incorrect assumptions or plausible but unsupported statements. NIST identifies this risk as confabulation and recommends evaluating generated outputs and verifying their supporting sources. In security assessment, a convincing explanation must not be mistaken for verified evidence. [3]

paragraphs.text: ThreatLens is motivated by the need to connect these activities within a practical review environment. It brings project submission, automated analysis, source inspection, finding review, remediation guidance and reporting into one workflow. Its purpose is to help developers understand what was reported, examine the available evidence and decide what to investigate next. Human review remains necessary throughout this process.

paragraphs.text: An automated security finding is useful only when the developer can relate it to the application being reviewed. A warning that names a vulnerability category without showing its source location or supporting evidence leaves important questions unanswered. The developer still needs to establish whether the affected code receives untrusted input, whether relevant safeguards exist and whether the reported operation can be reached under realistic conditions.

paragraphs.text: For example, the presence of a potentially dangerous HTML operation does not, by itself, demonstrate cross-site scripting. The interpretation changes depending on whether the assigned content is a fixed, trusted value or contains attacker-controlled data. A useful assessment should distinguish the observed operation from assumptions about input control and runtime behaviour. Otherwise, an automated warning may lead to unnecessary changes or distract attention from a more significant issue.

paragraphs.text: Prioritisation introduces a related difficulty. Severity labels and Common Vulnerability Scoring System scores help communicate technical characteristics, but they do not independently establish the operational importance of every finding. FIRST describes CVSS as a severity framework and notes that vulnerability management also requires organisational and environmental considerations. ThreatLens must therefore present available severity information without implying that a numerical score proves exploitation or completely describes business risk. [4]

paragraphs.text: The review process also has practical reliability requirements. Uploaded archives are untrusted inputs. Source previews may still be preparing while analysis continues, and external services may become unavailable. Users may leave a page before a scan finishes or reopen an audit after its source-preview window expires. These conditions must be explained accurately. An incomplete scan must not appear clean, and an unavailable preview must not erase saved findings.

paragraphs.text: The problem addressed by this project is therefore to develop a source-code assessment platform that combines automated checks with understandable, traceable review. The platform must preserve the relationship between a finding and its evidence, provide useful remediation guidance, control access to private project data and make analysis limitations visible. It must support investigation without presenting automated output as a guarantee that an application is secure.

paragraphs.text: Manual code review allows a reviewer to consider application purpose, expected behaviour and business rules. It is valuable where security depends on context that is difficult to express through a general rule. Its effectiveness, however, depends on reviewer knowledge, available time and familiarity with the project. Maintaining consistent review coverage across a growing codebase can be difficult.

paragraphs.text: Rule-based scanners provide repeatable checks for defined patterns. Their output can help reviewers focus on relevant files, but different tools may describe similar issues using different categories or evidence formats. Bringing those results together requires more than displaying them in one list. The system must preserve distinct findings, handle genuine duplicates and retain the information needed to understand where each result originated.

paragraphs.text: Conversational assistants can help explain a finding, but a general conversation may not include the exact source version, saved evidence or application context. A response can consequently recommend a change that does not match the recorded problem. ThreatLens addresses this concern by linking finding-specific guidance to authorised audit context and keeping suggested replacement code separate from recorded evidence.

paragraphs.text: Compliance review adds requirements that cannot always be inferred from source code. Browser extensions illustrate this distinction clearly. Chrome Web Store policies apply to the wider extension experience, including declarations and marketing materials. Microsoft Edge Add-ons policies also address matters such as permissions, privacy, functionality and browser-setting changes. A packaged ZIP can provide evidence for some checks, while other requirements need developer declarations or manual assessment. [5] [6]

paragraphs.text: This study addresses an integration and evaluation gap: how to connect automated security results with a review process that remains understandable, traceable and appropriately bounded. The work does not assume that existing scanners or development platforms lack all such capabilities. Instead, it examines how these requirements can be implemented together within ThreatLens and verified against the project’s intended workflows.

paragraphs.text: The first area concerns evidence continuity. A finding should remain connected to its audit, file location and available source excerpt as the user moves between the Workbench, Findings, Attack Graph, Security Advisor and Reports. If these views show inconsistent counts or disconnected details, the reviewer may struggle to determine which result is authoritative. Maintaining this continuity is therefore a system requirement as well as an interface concern.

paragraphs.text: The second area concerns the interpretation of remediation guidance. An explanation should make clear what was observed, what remains uncertain and why a suggested change may be relevant. Generated code also needs to remain visibly separate from the original source. Producing a suggestion must not imply that the change has been applied, tested or proven to remove the underlying issue.

Producing a suggestion must not imply that the change has been applied, tested or proven to remove the underlying issue. </w:t>
  </w:r>
</w:p>

paragraphs.text: The third area concerns coverage and evaluation. Completing an analysis job does not establish that every file, vulnerability class or policy requirement was assessed. Similarly, functional tests do not demonstrate universal detection accuracy. ThreatLens therefore needs explicit coverage information and an evaluation approach that separates workflow correctness, access control, evidence consistency and detection quality.

paragraphs.text: These questions guide both implementation and evaluation. Evidence consistency and workflow behaviour can be examined through repeatable tests. Claims about detection precision or recall require independently labelled examples and a defined assessment procedure. Interface usability also requires suitable evaluation; the presence of a feature alone does not establish that users find it understandable.

paragraphs.text: ThreatLens focuses on the assessment of submitted source projects and the review of saved results. The main workflow accepts project ZIP archives, prepares available source previews and presents recorded findings through a read-only workbench. Supporting pages provide finding filters, triage, evidence relationships, contextual guidance and report downloads. Repository-related capabilities depend on the required GitHub configuration and the acting user’s permissions.

paragraphs.text: The project also supports review of built browser-extension ZIPs for Chrome Web Store and Microsoft Edge Add-ons. This review considers package evidence and supplied declarations against versioned policy references. It distinguishes detected violations from checks that need manual review, remain unassessed or are not applicable. The platform does not install extensions, inspect the developer’s actual browser settings or submit packages to either store.

paragraphs.text: Assessment is limited by the available source, supported analysis methods, input limits and configured services. Static review cannot establish every runtime condition or business-logic requirement. Model-assisted explanations may also contain mistakes. A report with no recorded findings therefore describes the outcome of the performed assessment, not proof that the project contains no security weaknesses.

paragraphs.text: Vulnerability detection attempts to identify conditions that may allow software to behave insecurely. A useful assessment distinguishes a suspicious construct from a demonstrated vulnerability. The meaning of an alert depends on data flow, validation, configuration and runtime conditions.

paragraphs.text: Different analysis methods provide different forms of evidence. Some recognise known patterns, while others reason about dependencies, source relationships or likely behaviour. Human review remains important because an automated tool may not have enough information to determine whether a reported condition is reachable or exploitable.

paragraphs.text: The usefulness of static analysis depends on the supported language, rules and available context. Framework-specific behaviour, dynamic execution and incomplete source information can limit the analysis. A reported pattern should therefore lead to investigation rather than an automatic claim that exploitation is possible.

    <w:t>These tasks require different evidence. A package finding needs reliable version information, whereas a suspected secret requires contextual interpretation. A token-shaped string may be a placeholder, a test value or a genuine credential. </w:t>

paragraphs.text: SecretBench provides a labelled dataset intended to support research on software-secret detection [2]. Its methodological relevance is that evaluation requires both genuine examples and misleading look-alike values. A collection containing only successful detections cannot adequately measure false alarms.

paragraphs.text: However, finding a relevant passage and interpreting it correctly are separate tasks. Retrieval supplies context; it does not independently verify a vulnerability or settle a compliance question. The reference source and the reasoning behind each proposed relationship must remain available for inspection.

paragraphs.text: Remediation guidance has a similar limitation. A recommendation should identify its assumptions, expected behavioural effects and suggested verification steps. ThreatLens treats both mapping and remediation as assistance for a reviewer rather than a substitute for professional assessment.

paragraphs.text: Requirements should be assigned identifiers and connected to test cases. Reopening a completed audit, for example, concerns persistence. Pankaj Sonewane, for his guidance and direction to support during the development of ThreatLens Software. His feedback during project to discussions helped us to improve our and address the technical challenges, and present our work more efficiently. We are also thankful to the faculty and staff of G H Raisoni College of Engineering, Nagpur, for providing the facilities and academic environment, computational resources and administration. We also acknowledge the researchers, open-source contributors and standards organizations whose published research, technical documentation and security frameworks compliance supported the development of ThreatLens(Archon) Software. Their contributions provided valuable insights into vulnerability detection, code analysis, RAG, CVSS-based risk assessment and remediation recommendations. Responsibility for the system architecture, database Security implementation, experimental evaluation, and audit security  and conclusions in solution format ai automated way. We are grateful to our families and friends for their patience, encouragement and support during the development, we acknowledge the effort of every member of the project team in maintaining the code, reviewing, testing and preparing the manuscript and thesis, and completing the work collaboratively. ABSTRACT Security assessment is often treated as a separate activity from software development. Developers may receive vulnerability reports that identify a problem but provide little context about the affected code, its potential impact, or the steps needed to address it. Compliance requirements add another challenge, particularly when technical findings must be connected to documented controls or browser-extension store policies. These gaps make security review difficult to interpret and act upon, especially for s mall development teams. This thesis presents ThreatLens, a web-based platform that brings codebase auditing, threat modeling, compliance assessment, and remediation guidance into a single workflow. Users can submit project archives for analysis and examine saved results through a read-only, editor-style workbench. The platform combines static security checks with language-model-assisted analysis to identify potential weaknesses and provide explanations grounded in available source evidence. Findings include severity, recorded file  locations, relevant code excerpts, and remediation guidance. The workbench connects source files with findings, control mappings, and suggested verification steps. An evidence-based graph helps users explore relationships between findings and affected components without presenting those relationships as confirmed exploitation paths. Security Advisor provides contextual explanations and code suggestions, while keeping proposed changes separate from the uploaded source. Browser-extension reviews extend this workflow to Chrome Web Store and Microsoft Edge Add-ons polici es, distinguishing detected violations from requirements that need manual review or cannot be assessed from the submitted package. ThreatLens also provides saved audit history, finding triage, comparison of compatible extension reviews, and downloadable reports. Workspace authorization, private source storage, evidence redaction, and time-limited source previews support controlled access to sensitive project information. Verification covers automated regressions, access-control checks, report generation, and representative browser workflows; these checks establish functional behavior rather than proving universal vulnerability-detectio n accuracy. The principal contribution is an integrated, traceable review workflow that helps developers move from a reported concern to its supporting evidence, possible remedy, and verification approach. ThreatLens supports informed security decisions, but does not replace manual testing, professional assessment, or official compliance and store-approval processes. Keywords: Codebase Security Auditing; Static Analysis; Threat Modeling; Compliance Assessment; Large Language Models; Secure Software Development. APPENDIX E ADDITIONAL TECHNICAL EVIDENCE 12   CHAPTER 1 INTRODUCTION 1.1 Background and Motivation  Software applications manage personal information, business transactions, communication and access to essential services. Their security depends partly on decisions made during development, including how inputs are validated, database queries are constructed, permissions are enforced and sensitive information is stored. A weakness in these areas can expose information or allow unintended operations. Security assessment must therefore form part of software development rather than being treated only as a final check before deployment. The Secure Software Development Framework published by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) supports integrating security practices throughout the software development life cycle.  [1]   Reviewing source code becomes more demanding as projects grow across multiple files, frameworks and dependencies. A developer investigating a warning may need to locate the affected statement, understand the surrounding code and determine whether the reported condition is relevant to the application. Finding a potentially unsafe operation is only one part of this process. The reviewer must also decide what evidence supports the finding and how a proposed correction can be checked without changing the intended behaviour.  Static Application Security Testing helps identify suspicious code patterns without running the application. It provides a useful starting point for reviewing concerns such as injection, unsafe output handling and exposed credentials. However, a reported pattern is not necessarily an exploitable vulnerability. Static analysis can produce false positives and may miss problems that depend on runtime conditions, application state or business logic. Its results therefore require interpretation and verification.  [2]   Language models offer another form of assistance by explaining code and suggesting possible remedies. These capabilities are useful when a finding is technically correct but difficult for a developer to understand. Nevertheless, generated explanations can contain incorrect assumptions or plausible but unsupported statements. NIST identifies this risk as confabulation and recommends evaluating generated outputs and verifying  their supporting sources. In security assessment, a convincing explanation must not be mistaken for verified evidence.  [3]   ThreatLens is motivated by the need to connect these activities within a practical review environment. It brings project submission, automated analysis, source inspection, finding review, remediation guidance and reporting into one workflow. Its purpose is to help developers understand what was reported, examine the available evidence and decide what to investigate next. Human review remains necessary throughout this process.  1.2 Problem Statement  An automated security finding is useful only when the developer can relate it to the application being reviewed. A warning that names a vulnerability category without showing its source location or supporting evidence leaves important questions unanswered. The developer still needs to establish whether the affected code receives untrusted input, whether relevant safeguards exist and whether the reported operation can be reached under realistic conditions.  For example, the presence of a potentially dangerous HTML operation does not, by itself, demonstrate cross-site scripting. The interpretation changes depending on whether the assigned content is a fixed, trusted value or contains attacker-controlled data. A useful assessment should distinguish the observed operation from assumptions about input control and runtime behaviour. Otherwise, an automated warning may lead to unnecessary changes or distract attention from a more significant issue.  Prioritisation introduces a related difficulty. Severity labels and Common Vulnerability Scoring System scores help communicate technical characteristics, but they do not independently establish the operational importance of every finding. FIRST describes CVSS as a severity framework and notes that vulnerability management also requires organisational and environmental considerations. ThreatLens must therefore present available severity information without implying that a numerical score proves exploitation or completely describes business risk.  [4]   The review process also has practical reliability requirements. Uploaded archives are untrusted inputs. Source previews may still be preparing while analysis continues, and external services may become unavailable. Users may leave a page before a scan finishes or reopen an audit after its source-preview window expires. These conditions must be explained accurately. An incomplete scan must not appear clean, and an unavailable preview must not erase saved findings.  The problem addressed by this project is therefore to develop a source-code assessment platform that combines automated checks with understandable, traceable review. The platform must preserve the relationship between a finding and its evidence, provide useful remediation guidance, control access to private project data and make analysis limitations visible. It must support investigation without presenting automated output as a guarantee that an application is secure.  1.3 Existing Approaches and Challenges  Manual code review allows a reviewer to consider application purpose, expected behaviour and business rules. It is valuable where security depends on context that is difficult to express through a general rule. Its effectiveness, however, depends on reviewer knowledge, available time and familiarity with the project. Maintaining consistent review coverage across a growing codebase can be difficult.  Rule-based scanners provide repeatable checks for defined patterns. Their output can help reviewers focus on relevant files, but different tools may describe similar issues using different categories or evidence formats. Bringing those results together requires more than displaying them in one list. The system must preserve distinct findings, handle genuine duplicates and retain the information needed to understand where each result originated.  Conversational assistants can help explain a finding, but a general conversation may not include the exact source version, saved evidence or application context. A response can consequently recommend a change that does not match the recorded problem. ThreatLens addresses this concern by linking finding-specific guidance to authorised audit context and keeping suggested replacement code separate from recorded evidence.  Compliance review adds requirements that cannot always be inferred from source code. Browser extensions illustrate this distinction clearly. Chrome Web Store policies apply to the wider extension experience, including declarations and marketing materials. Microsoft Edge Add-ons policies also address matters such as permissions, privacy, functionality and browser-setting changes. A packaged ZIP can provide evidence for some checks, while other requirements need developer declarations or manual assessment.  [5]   [6]   These approaches serve different purposes. The challenge for ThreatLens is to connect them without hiding their differences. A scanner result, a model-generated suggestion, a compliance mapping and a reviewer decision should remain distinguishable even when they appear in the same interface.  1.4 Research Gap  This study addresses an integration and evaluation gap: how to connect automated security results with a review process that remains understandable, traceable and appropriately bounded. The work does not assume that existing scanners or development platforms lack all such capabilities. Instead, it examines how these requirements can be implemented together within ThreatLens and verified against the project’s intended workflows.  The first area concerns evidence continuity. A finding should remain connected to its audit, file location and available source excerpt as the user moves between the Workbench, Findings, Attack Graph, Security Advisor and Reports. If these views show inconsistent counts or disconnected details, the reviewer may struggle to determine which result is authoritative. Maintaining this continuity is therefore a system requirement as well as an interface concern.  The second area concerns the interpretation of remediation guidance. An explanation should make clear what was observed, what remains uncertain and why a suggested change may be relevant. Generated code also needs to remain visibly separate from the original source. Producing a suggestion must not imply that the change has been applied, tested or proven to remove the underlying issue.  The third area concerns coverage and evaluation. Completing an analysis job does not establish that every file, vulnerability class or policy requirement was assessed. Similarly, functional tests do not demonstrate universal detection accuracy. ThreatLens therefore needs explicit coverage information and an evaluation approach that separates workflow correctness, access control, evidence consistency and detection quality.  The research gap addressed by the thesis is consequently the practical design and verification of an integrated assessment workflow with these distinctions intact. Its contribution is evaluated through the implemented system and supporting evidence, rather than through an unsupported claim that combining existing tools automatically produces superior security results.  1.5 Aim and Objectives  The aim of this project is to develop and evaluate ThreatLens as an AI-assisted framework for automated source-code security assessment, vulnerability prioritisation and compliance analysis, with source-based evidence and human review at the centre of the workflow.  The project objectives are:  To provide an authenticated project-submission workflow that validates supported inputs and prepares source material for assessment.  To combine static security checks with language-model-assisted analysis while retaining finding provenance and relevant source evidence.  To organise findings into a consistent representation that supports file locations, vulnerability categories, available severity information and review status.  To develop a read-only Audit Workbench through which users can inspect source files, findings, remediation steps and suggested verification activities.  To provide contextual explanations and on-demand code suggestions that remain separate from uploaded source and require review before use.  To present evidence relationships and applicable compliance mappings without treating them as confirmed attack paths or proof of compliance.  To support saved audit history, controlled access, report generation and the reopening of results across the audit lifecycle.  To evaluate functional behaviour, evidence consistency, access restrictions, failure handling and interface responsiveness using documented test cases and appropriate fixtures.  Together, these objectives establish a sequence from safe submission to evidence-based review and reporting. They do not include unrestricted execution of uploaded projects, autonomous acceptance of generated fixes or guaranteed detection of every vulnerability.  1.6 Research Questions  The study is guided by the following research questions.  RQ1.  How can static security checks and language-model-assisted analysis be combined while preserving the source location, provenance and supporting evidence of each finding?  RQ2.  How can an editor-style workbench present findings, severity information and remediation guidance so that users can distinguish recorded facts from assumptions and generated suggestions?  RQ3.  How can security findings and compliance assessments be presented together without confusing vulnerability severity, policy outcomes and unassessed requirements?  RQ4.  How reliably does the implemented workflow handle authorised access, incomplete scans, unavailable services, source expiry and the reopening of saved results?  These questions guide both implementation and evaluation. Evidence consistency and workflow behaviour can be examined through repeatable tests. Claims about detection precision or recall require independently labelled examples and a defined assessment  procedure. Interface usability also requires suitable evaluation; the presence of a feature alone does not establish that users find it understandable.  1.7 Project Scope and Limitations  ThreatLens focuses on the assessment of submitted source projects and the review of saved results. The main workflow accepts project ZIP archives, prepares available source previews and presents recorded findings through a read-only workbench. Supporting pages provide finding filters, triage, evidence relationships, contextual guidance and report downloads. Repository-related capabilities depend on the required GitHub configuration and the acting user’s permissions.  The project also supports review of built browser-extension ZIPs for Chrome Web Store and Microsoft Edge Add-ons. This review considers package evidence and supplied declarations against versioned policy references. It distinguishes detected violations from checks that need manual review, remain unassessed or are not applicable. The platform does not install extensions, inspect the developer’s actual browser settings or submit packages to either store.  Assessment is limited by the available source, supported analysis methods, input limits and configured services. Static review cannot establish every runtime condition or business-logic requirement. Model-assisted explanations may also contain mistakes. A report with no recorded findings therefore describes the outcome of the performed assessment, not proof that the project contains no security weaknesses.  Remediation suggestions remain subject to review and testing. For configured repository workflows, publishing follows a reviewed branch-and-pull-request process rather than an automatic change to the target branch. Creating a proposal, passing a structural check or opening a pull request does not independently establish that a finding has been resolved.  Project information is handled through authenticated workspace access and private source storage. Source previews follow a defined retention window, while saved findings and reports have separate history behaviour. Where external model services are used, their availability and data-handling configuration form part of the deployment  boundary. These constraints must be considered when selecting projects for assessment and interpreting the results.  1.8 Main Contributions   The principal contributions of the project are as follows.  Figure 1.1: Overall architecture of ThreatLens showing the application interface, authenticated API, source preparation, security analysis and private persistence.  Contribution 1. A useful assessment distinguishes a suspicious construct from a demonstrated vulnerability. The meaning of an alert depends on data flow, validation, configuration and runtime conditions.  Different analysis methods provide different forms of evidence. Some recognise known patterns, while others reason about dependencies, source relationships or likely behaviour. Human review remains important because an automated tool may not have enough information to determine whether a reported condition is reachable or exploitable.  This chapter considers these complementary methods and their relevance to ThreatLens. It does not assume that combining several tools automatically improves detection accuracy.  2.2 Static Application Security Testing (SAST)  Static analysis examines code without running the target application. Depending on the tool, it may use pattern matching, syntax trees, control-flow analysis or data-flow reasoning.  OWASP describes taint analysis as following untrusted data from a source towards a potentially dangerous sink [1]. This helps reviewers understand whether external input can reach a sensitive operation without appropriate handling.  The usefulness of static analysis depends on the supported language, rules and available context. Framework-specific behaviour, dynamic execution and incomplete source information can limit the analysis. A reported pattern should therefore lead to investigation rather than an automatic claim that exploitation is possible.  2.3 Dependency, Secret and Configuration Analysis  Dependency analysis examines the packages used by an application and their recorded versions. Secret detection looks for credentials or similar sensitive values. Configuration analysis examines settings that influence deployment and application behaviour.  These tasks require different evidence. A package finding needs reliable version information, whereas a suspected secret requires contextual interpretation. A token-shaped string may be a placeholder, a test value or a genuine credential.  SecretBench provides a labelled dataset intended to support research on software-secret detection [2]. Its methodological relevance is that evaluation requires both genuine examples and misleading look-alike values. A collection containing only successful detections cannot adequately measure false alarms.  2.4 AI and Large Language Models for Code Security  Language models can relate a code fragment to a natural-language explanation and suggest possible changes. Zhou and colleagues review research on their use in vulnerability detection and repair [3].  This literature provides a foundation for exploring model-assisted review, but it does not establish the accuracy of the provider, model or prompts selected for ThreatLens. Generated explanations must be checked against the submitted source.  The need for review becomes particularly important when the model receives only part of a file or lacks runtime context. A convincing explanation may still overstate the evidence, misunderstand an application-specific assumption or propose a change that alters intended behaviour.  2.5 Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Security Analysis  Retrieval-augmented generation combines generated responses with retrieved reference material. Lewis and colleagues describe an approach that incorporates an external retrieval mechanism into knowledge-intensive language tasks [4].  In security review, reference material may include weakness descriptions, secure-development guidance or control clauses. Retrieved passages can help explain why a finding may relate to a particular requirement.  However, finding a relevant passage and interpreting it correctly are separate tasks. Retrieval supplies context; it does not independently verify a vulnerability or settle a  compliance question. The reference source and the reasoning behind each proposed relationship must remain available for inspection.  2.6 Vulnerability Taxonomies and CVSS Prioritization  MITRE’s Common Weakness Enumeration provides a vocabulary for describing categories of software and hardware weaknesses [5]. It helps organise findings using consistent terminology.  The Common Vulnerability Scoring System serves a different purpose. CVSS characterises vulnerability severity through defined metrics [6]. A weakness identifier is not a severity score, and neither is a triage decision.  Keeping these concepts separate prevents misleading interpretations. A critical severity label describes potential seriousness under stated assumptions. An open status describes the current review state. A control mapping describes a possible relationship to a requirement. These fields should not be treated as interchangeable.  2.7 Compliance Mapping and Remediation Guidance  Compliance mapping links an observation to a potentially relevant requirement. A useful mapping explains why the requirement applies and identifies any supporting evidence that is still missing.  Many obligations concern organisational procedures, staff responsibilities or operational controls that cannot be established from a repository alone. Source inspection can support part of an assessment, but it cannot demonstrate every aspect of compliance.  Remediation guidance has a similar limitation. A recommendation should identify its assumptions, expected behavioural effects and suggested verification steps. ThreatLens treats both mapping and remediation as assistance for a reviewer rather than a substitute for professional assessment.  2.8 Comparison with Existing Security Assessment Tools  The comparison in this study is organised by method rather than unsupported product rankings.  Static analysis contributes repeatable rule-based checks. Dependency and secret tools provide specialised inspection. Model-assisted review contributes explanations and contextual reasoning. Manual review contributes application knowledge and judgement.  These roles overlap, but they are not interchangeable. ThreatLens is considered as a workflow that combines and presents evidence. Claims of better precision, recall or performance require controlled baseline experiments rather than a comparison of interface features.  Figure 2.1: Complementary security-review approaches and their evidence: static patterns, package versions, suspected credentials, configuration settings, model explanations and human judgement.   The diagram should connect these approaches to a common evidence-review stage. It should not contain unsupported performance percentages or product rankings.  2.9 Comparative Literature Synthesis  The selected sources address different levels of the problem. OWASP explains analysis practices [1]. SecretBench concerns evaluation data for a specialised detection task [2]. Zhou and colleagues synthesise research on model-based detection and repair [3].  Lewis and colleagues establish the retrieval-generation approach [4], while CWE and CVSS provide classification and severity terminology [5, 6].  Together, these sources support an evidence-oriented review design. However, none directly validates the combined ThreatLens deployment. The platform therefore requires its own evaluation of integration, correctness, coverage and user interaction.  2.10 Consolidated Research Gap  The resulting research focus is a traceable connection among source material, analysis outputs, control references and reviewer actions.  The study must also separate technical integration from demonstrated benefit. A platform may successfully combine tools while still producing unnecessary alerts or incomplete recommendations.  The research gap is therefore addressed through both implementation and an evaluation protocol. Coverage, detection quality, usability and operational behaviour must be assessed independently before broader claims can be made.    CHAPTER 3 METHODOLOGY 3.1 Research Design and Workflow   The study follows an engineering-development approach. Requirements are identified from the review tasks a developer must perform, translated into architecture and data contracts, and implemented through successive application components.  Verification examines both successful workflows and failure conditions. The final discussion relates the available evidence to the original objectives.  This approach allows implementation progress to be documented without presenting every completed feature as a validated research result.  Figure 3.1: Research workflow from problem definition and requirements to architecture, implementation, verification and discussion of limitations.   3.2 Functional and Non-Functional Requirements  Functional requirements include sign-in, workspace selection, project intake, progress display, finding inspection, source navigation, remediation guidance and report access.  Non-functional requirements include controlled resource use, readable interfaces, explicit failure states and protection of private material.  Requirements should be assigned identifiers and connected to test cases. Reopening a completed audit, for example, concerns persistence. Denying an outsider’s source  request concerns authorisation. These behaviours require different verification procedures even though both are necessary for a reliable application.  3.3 Test Project and Input Selection  Test inputs should include deliberately vulnerable fixtures, corrected versions of those fixtures and permitted real-world projects. Inputs should vary in language, size, directory structure, dependencies and supported file types.  Benign examples are necessary to examine false alarms. Selection must also avoid exposing live credentials or private code.  [AUTHOR INPUT: List the exact test projects, licences or permissions, versions, checksums and reasons for selection.]   The dataset description should identify whether each input is a synthetic fixture, an open-source project or a private project used with permission.  3.4 Source Code Ingestion and Preprocessing  The intake process validates the submitted archive before preparing files for inspection. Paths, archive expansion and supported content require checks because uploads are untrusted.  A manifest records files available for preview, while analysis may use a smaller eligible subset. Preprocessing must preserve the relationship between a saved finding and its original source coordinates.  Excluded or truncated material belongs in the coverage record. It should not disappear from the explanation of what the system analysed.  3.5 Static Scanning and Finding Normalization  Analysis outputs are normalised into records that can be displayed consistently. A useful record includes an identifier, severity, description, source location, provenance and any available weakness or remediation information.  Normalisation must preserve distinctions in the original evidence. Two alerts with the same title are not necessarily duplicates. Similarly, an empty result after scanner failure is not equivalent to a successful check with no findings.  Duplicate handling and error interpretation therefore require explicit test cases.  3.6 LLM-Assisted Analysis and RAG  Model-assisted analysis receives bounded context and returns information for review. Repository text is treated as data, not as instructions that can redefine the task.  For a configured retrieval experiment, relevant reference passages are supplied alongside the finding, with identifiers retained for inspection. The study should record the provider, model, prompt version, context limits and reference-corpus version.  The local API profile alone does not establish that the separate retrieval stack was installed or exercised. Results must identify the actual configuration used.  3.7 Severity Scoring and Compliance Mapping  Severity, weakness classification and control mapping are evaluated separately. A score needs a defensible metric vector, while a control mapping needs an identifiable source and a reason for applicability.  Missing values remain unavailable rather than being converted into harmless scores. Reviewers should record disagreements and the reasoning used to resolve them.  Framework assessment signals are presented as automated interpretations of available evidence, not as statements that an organisation satisfies every requirement.  3.8 Remediation and Report Generation  Written remediation is retained alongside the finding. A code solution, where requested, is presented as a proposed replacement and must not be confused with uploaded source.  Reports are assembled from saved assessment data so that exporting a document does not silently trigger a new analysis. Evaluation should compare displayed findings with exported content, including source locations, limitations and missing fields.  Private Advisor conversations should not be introduced into shared audit output during report preparation.  3.9 Evaluation Protocol  Each run should record the application revision, input checksum, configuration, active engines and timestamps.  Functional tests examine workflow behaviour. Access-control tests examine permitted and denied actions. Labelled detection tests examine correctness.  Repeated timing runs should use the same machine and comparable network conditions where practical. Model and baseline settings should be fixed before the final evaluation. Failures and skipped integrations must remain in the record rather than being excluded to improve the apparent outcome.  3.10 Evaluation Metrics  Detection quality is measured using independently labelled reference cases.  Let:  TP represent correctly identified labelled defects.  FP represent incorrectly reported defects.  FN represent labelled defects that were missed.  The metrics are:  Precision = TP / (TP + FP)   Recall = TP / (TP + FN)   F1-score = 2TP / (2TP + FP + FN)   A zero denominator should be handled using a stated convention rather than silently treated as a perfect result.  Timing metrics should distinguish acceptance-to-first-preview, analysis, persistence and end-to-end completion. Coverage should report analysed files against eligible files, with exclusions explained.  3.11 Ethical and Security Considerations  Only authorised projects should be uploaded. Source code, credentials and conversations require controlled access. Any use of an external provider should be disclosed to the project owner.  Public thesis figures should remove identifying account details without altering the assessment results. Tests involving deletion or publishing must use isolated resources.  The study should distinguish actual observations from illustrative diagrams, test fixtures and proposed future work. Relevant writing or analytical assistance should be disclosed according to institutional requirements.    CHAPTER 4 DATA COLLECTION, TOOLS AND COMPUTATIONAL PLATFORM 4.1 Hardware and Operating Environment   Hardware information is necessary for interpreting performance. Each source should be used only for the type of claim it can establish.  4.9 Reproducibility and Version Control  A reproducible record connects each input to a repository revision, dependency configuration, active feature flags, model selection and output set.  Useful artefacts include sanitised configuration summaries, input checksums, commands, timestamps and structured test results. Public records must exclude secrets and private source material.  Screenshots should carry a capture date and identify demonstration data where applicable. Repeating a run under changed provider behaviour or reference material should be treated as a new experimental condition.    CHAPTER 5 SYSTEM DESIGN AND IMPLEMENTATION 5.1 Overall ThreatLens Architecture   The architecture separates user interaction, request authorisation, analysis, source preparation and persistent results.  The browser requests operations through the API, while saved audit records allow users to revisit results. Source preparation and analysis have independent progress because uploading a readable preview is not the same as completing security checks.  Figure 1.1 provides the system overview. It is referenced here rather than repeated, keeping this chapter focused on implementation decisions and two essential interface figures.  5.2 User Interface and Application Navigation  The navigation follows the review workflow through Dashboard, Codebase Audit, Findings, Workbench, Attack Graph, Reports and Security Advisor.  History and resume controls help users return to saved work. Settings and profile controls are separate from the assessment itself.  The interface should explain whether a view shows the latest completed audit, a selected historical scan or an example scenario. This distinction prevents users from interpreting an empty or still-running scan as a clean assessment.  5.3 Authentication, Authorization and Workspaces  Authentication identifies the user, while authorisation determines which workspace resources that user may access.  The application must check resource relationships rather than trusting identifiers supplied by the browser. Database policies provide an additional boundary, while privileged server credentials remain outside client bundles.  A viewer’s ability to read shared findings does not imply permission to delete scans or publish repository changes. These distinctions require verification through actual permitted and denied requests.  5.4 Local In-Process Scanning Pipeline  The saved-ZIP path accepts an authorised upload, prepares scan state and starts source handling and analysis.  Available previews can be published while remaining files are still being prepared. Findings should become final only after persistence succeeds. A source-preparation failure must not erase otherwise saved findings.  Returning to the intake page uses an account- and workspace-scoped reference to reopen the audit. The lifetime of an accepted scan is therefore separate from the lifetime of the upload component.  5.5 Hosted Scanning and Worker-Orchestrated Pipeline  The repository also documents a separate scanner-worker deployment with additional dependencies and services.  A worker architecture can move long-running tasks away from API processes, but requires explicit job ownership, recovery and service configuration. It is a deployment option, not proof that the current saved-ZIP path uses the same orchestration.  [AUTHOR INPUT: Identify whether the worker deployment was exercised, including broker, worker and service versions. Otherwise, state that it was not evaluated.]   5.6 Static Scanning Engines and Finding Normalization  Normalised findings allow the interface to present severity, location, origin and remediation consistently across supported inputs.  Stable finding identifiers remain important when titles or source locations are similar. Counts and pagination must refer to saved records, not only to the rows currently displayed.  An engine failure should contribute a limitation to the scan. An unsupported language should remain outside any claim of complete coverage. The actual engine set must be documented for each execution mode.  5.7 AI Agent Pipeline and Prompt Design  Model assistance is used to interpret findings and prepare guidance from bounded context.  A finding-specific request must preserve the authorised workspace, scan and finding relationship. It should not silently become a general conversation after losing its context.  Prompts should separate observations, assumptions, suggested changes and verification steps. The interface also needs explicit handling for interrupted responses. A truncated code suggestion remains incomplete even when its opening explanation appears convincing.  5.8 CVSS Scoring and Vulnerability Classification  The interface preserves recorded weakness identifiers and available scores. CVSS 3.1 defines severity through a metric vector [6]. A valid zero score is therefore different from a missing score.  A model-generated score should be checked for consistency with its vector and supporting evidence.  Triage decisions, such as accepting risk or marking a false positive, remain separate from severity. Creating a fix proposal or downloading a report must not automatically change a finding’s triage state.  5.9 RAG and Compliance Mapping  The repository contains retrieval components, including embedding, vector-client and corpus-preparation modules. Their presence establishes implementation material, not successful execution in the current local mode.  A retrieval-enabled assessment should preserve the corpus version, retrieved control identifiers and evidence supporting each proposed relationship.  When a required service is unavailable, that limitation should be reported. A saved framework percentage must not be presented as legal compliance or certification.  5.10 Scan Visualization and Attack Graph  The workbench places the file explorer, source viewer and finding details within one page. A reviewer can inspect the reported location while retaining access to evidence and remediation.  The graph provides a complementary view of relationships between findings and source components. In the saved-evidence view, connectors represent associations rather than verified network routes or successful exploitation.  Illustrative scenarios must remain explicitly labelled and separate from the user’s saved evidence.  Figure 5.1: Read-only Audit Workbench showing source navigation, a selected finding and its recorded evidence. Figure 5.2: Attack Graph interface using isolated test-fixture data: (a) source associations and graph controls; (b) selected finding evidence and remediation guidance. Connections do not establish confirmed exploitability. .   Use clear screenshots from the actual application. These are the only two figures required in Chapter 5.  5.11 Reporting, Exports and Audit Events  Reports organise completed saved audits and prepare PDFs on demand. The exported document should preserve the same finding identities, evidence and limitations shown in the interface.  Audit events record actions and state transitions, whereas scan history records saved assessments. They should not be described as interchangeable.  Export verification must examine all selected or filtered results rather than assuming that one visible page contains the entire dataset. A report communicates assessment evidence; it is not an approval certificate.  5.12 Database Schema and Data Relationships  Workspaces connect members to scans, and scans connect findings with source snapshots and related assessment information.  Optional conversation and repository features add relationships without changing the meaning of the core audit records.  Foreign keys and access policies serve different purposes. A valid database relationship does not, by itself, authorise the requesting user to read or modify the linked record. Both structural integrity and access enforcement are necessary.  5.13 API Design and Data Flow  API requests need a clear scope and a response appropriate to the operation. List endpoints return bounded summaries, while detailed evidence is loaded when selected.  Upload acceptance, scan completion and source availability require distinct states. Request failures should distinguish unavailable services, invalid credentials and denied access.  Safe-read recovery must not become automatic replay of uploads or publishing operations. API documentation should identify these behaviours without exposing credentials or private payloads.  5.14 Security and Reliability Controls  The documented design includes archive validation, private storage, source redaction, workspace checks, bounded processing and explicit error states.  Uploaded dependency files must not cause arbitrary package installation on the API host. Report generation restricts resource access, and code suggestions remain read-only until handled through a separately authorised workflow.  These controls require dedicated verification, including malformed inputs and revoked access. No single scanner run, unit-test suite or successful deployment establishes that every security boundary works.  5.15 Deployment and Configuration  The frontend builds as a standalone Node.js server, while the API runs separately.  Both services must refer to the intended identity project, and browser origins must match the API’s permitted configuration. Optional integrations are enabled only when their services and credentials are configured.  Installation profiles should be reproduced in isolated environments. Public frontend configuration and server-only secrets must remain distinct. Actual environment-file values, passwords and access tokens must never appear in the thesis.    CHAPTER 6 TESTING AND SUMMARY OF RESULTS 6.1 Experimental Environment  This chapter distinguishes documented interface observations from quantitative experiments. The available figure notes describe captures made on 12 November 2026, but those captures do not constitute a complete regression report.  A defensible experimental record must identify the evaluated application revision and active deployment mode.  [AUTHOR INPUT: Insert the environment from Section 4.1, run identifiers, provider/model, enabled engines, corpus version where relevant, and commands used for the final evaluation.]   The environment description should make it possible to distinguish local processing from externally hosted services.  6.2 Test Dataset and Ground Truth  Ground truth is the reference against which detection claims are judged. It should identify each intentionally introduced or independently confirmed weakness, its location, expected behaviour and corrected counterpart.  Saved alerts cannot independently supply this reference because they are the outputs being evaluated.  [AUTHOR INPUT: Provide the labelled test inventory, reviewer procedure and policy for ambiguous cases.]   Real project names may be anonymised where necessary. However, the selection method and limitations of the dataset must remain clear.  6.3 Functional Test Cases  Functional verification should cover sign-in, workspace selection, upload acceptance, progressive source access, history reopening, finding selection, remediation guidance and report export.  Negative cases include malformed archives, unavailable providers, expired previews and denied workspace access.  A screenshot can demonstrate a visible state, but it does not show every transition that led to that state. Actual outcomes should be recorded with supporting evidence.  Test case   Expected behaviour   Observed result and evidence   Accepted ZIP followed by navigation to another page  Reopen the same server-side scan without duplicate submission  [AUTHOR INPUT]  Finding selected in the workbench  Correct evidence and source location remain associated  [AUTHOR INPUT]  Provider or source-preview failure  Explicit limitation without a false clean or completed state  [AUTHOR INPUT]  Viewer and outsider requests  Only authorised reads and actions are permitted  [AUTHOR INPUT]  PDF export  Saved finding identities and limitations match the report  [AUTHOR INPUT]  6.4 Vulnerability Detection Results  The existing capture notes describe a saved MERN project audit with six reported findings. They also distinguish 90 preview entries from 81 scanned files.  These figures describe saved output. They do not establish six independently confirmed vulnerabilities or provide an accuracy measure.  The difference between preview count and analysed-file count illustrates why coverage must be reported separately from source availability.  [AUTHOR INPUT: Insert verified detection counts from the labelled evaluation. If unavailable, retain this section as an explicitly limited review of saved output.]   Figure 6.1: Saved audit report excerpt showing recorded source evidence, remediation and suggested verification checks. The excerpt illustrates reporting behaviour, not independently validated detection accuracy.   6.5 Detection Quality Metrics  Precision, recall and F1 should be calculated only after comparing findings with the labelled reference.  Duplicate alerts need a documented matching rule so that repeated reports do not inflate true positives. Historical manuscript totals should not be reused without their underlying evaluation records and matching procedure.  [AUTHOR INPUT: Supply TP, FP, FN, matching rules and per-language or per-category results.]   If these records are unavailable, the thesis should state that detection quality has not yet been established rather than presenting an estimated accuracy value.  6.6 Performance and Scan Duration  Useful timing separates waiting for acceptance, obtaining a readable source preview, analysing content and saving the final result.  Repeated runs should report the number of observations and a suitable summary, such as the median and range.  Concurrent stages can overlap. Their durations must not simply be added and presented as elapsed completion time. Differences between phase timings and total duration require recorded timing boundaries rather than assumed overhead.  [AUTHOR INPUT: Insert traceable run measurements, the number of repetitions and the exact timing boundaries.]   6.7 AI, RAG and Remediation Evaluation  Explanations should be reviewed for groundedness, uncertainty, correct source references and whether the proposed change preserves behaviour.  The saved SVG-related example is useful because static trusted markup must not automatically be equated with attacker-controlled HTML. A suggestion that overstates the evidence is a review failure even if its wording appears polished.  Retrieval evaluation requires labelled relevant controls. Repair evaluation requires applicable changes and appropriate tests.  [AUTHOR INPUT: Supply reviewer ratings, disagreements, relevance judgements and verified remediation examples.]   6.8 Robustness, Security and Error Handling  Robustness testing should deliberately interrupt the normal workflow. Relevant cases include unsafe archives, removed membership, expired source access, interrupted responses and unavailable services.  Each case requires an expected outcome and observed evidence.  A backend outage must not be mistaken for an invalid user session. Similarly, a scanner failure must not be counted as a successful clean scan.  The final assessment of these controls must refer to recorded tests. Application documentation and screenshots alone cannot establish that the failure paths behave correctly.  6.9 Comparison with Baselines  A useful baseline comparison would evaluate static-only analysis and the combined workflow on the same labelled inputs.  Where retrieval is studied, retrieval-enabled and non-retrieval conditions should use matched model settings and clearly defined relevance labels. Timing conditions should also remain comparable.  [AUTHOR INPUT: Insert actual baseline results or state that no controlled baseline experiment was completed.]   A feature comparison or literature survey cannot establish that ThreatLens is faster or more accurate than another system.  6.10 Discussion and Limitations  The available material supports a discussion of workflow design and saved-output presentation. It does not establish universal vulnerability detection, compliance correctness or superiority over other tools.  Important limitations include incomplete runtime context, partial file coverage, dependence on external services and the need for reviewer judgement.  The final thesis should identify which research questions have direct experimental answers and which remain open. A limited conclusion supported by evidence is more defensible than a broad claim based only on successful demonstrations.    CHAPTER 7 CONCLUSION 7.1 Summary of Achieved Objectives  The documented implementation brings project intake, source review, findings, guidance and reporting into one workspace-oriented application. Existing captures illustrate several of these interfaces with saved output.  The distinction between source availability and analysis completion is particularly important. It allows progress to be communicated without claiming that an unfinished assessment is clean.  Completion of each objective should be supported by the test evidence in Chapter 6 rather than inferred from the presence of an application page.  7.2 Key Findings and Contributions  The main engineering contribution is a traceable review workflow. Recorded evidence remains distinct from proposed changes, while the graph and reports offer complementary ways to inspect saved results.  The study also identifies an important evaluation distinction: preview coverage, analysed-file coverage, finding counts and detection accuracy are different quantities.  Treating these separately makes both the interface and the research discussion easier to understand. Quantitative improvements remain conditional on a completed and reproducible evaluation.  Figure 7.1: Summary of project objectives, corresponding implementation evidence and remaining validation needs.   The figure should use three columns: Objective, Available Evidence and Remaining Verification. Do not mark an objective as passed without its corresponding test record.  7.3 Limitations and Final Remarks  ThreatLens should be understood as assistance for developers and reviewers, not an automatic security authority.  Its usefulness depends on the quality of inputs, active analysis components and the care with which findings are interpreted. A repository cannot demonstrate every organisational control, and generated guidance cannot replace testing.  The project provides a basis for further evaluation while keeping these limitations visible. Its strongest supported contribution is the integration of review tasks, not a guarantee that uploaded software is secure.    CHAPTER 8 FUTURE SCOPE 8.1 Scanning Coverage and Language Support  Future work should broaden language and framework coverage through explicit parser support and documented rules.  Cross-file reasoning and runtime-aware validation may address cases that isolated snippets cannot explain. New capabilities should include benign examples, vulnerable fixtures and clear exclusion rules.  Packaged extensions and infrastructure configurations require their own assessment profiles. They should not be described as fully covered merely because their files can be uploaded.  8.2 AI and Retrieval Improvements  Model and retrieval improvements should begin with evaluation data rather than an assumption that a larger model will perform better.  Useful directions include versioned control corpora, relevance judgements, prompt comparisons and checks for unsupported explanations.  Context selection should preserve the evidence needed to investigate a finding while respecting privacy and input limits. Claims of reduced hallucination or improved remediation require measured comparisons, including cases where no code change is justified.  8.3 Continuous Integration and Workflow Automation  Repository scanning and reviewed publishing are already described as configurable capabilities. Future work should therefore focus on extending and validating them rather than presenting them as entirely absent.  Potential directions include policy-controlled continuous-integration initiation, clearer review checkpoints and reliable comparison after changes.  Publishing must retain explicit approval. Passing external checks must not automatically resolve a finding. Deployment and permission constraints should be tested in isolated repositories before broader use.  8.4 Scalability, Security and Deployment  Further deployment work should evaluate queueing, worker isolation, concurrent uploads, storage cleanup and recovery under load.  Performance improvements must not weaken authorisation or omit checks without disclosure. Operational evaluation should include provider outages, rate limits and membership changes during active work.  Browser-extension policy packs will also require version maintenance as store requirements change. The objective is controlled and observable behaviour under realistic conditions, not merely a lower duration from one benchmark run.  8.5 Extended Validation and User Studies  The next research stage should use diverse, independently labelled projects and participants with different levels of security experience.  A user study could measure the time required to locate evidence, the ability to distinguish suggestions from confirmed results, and the correctness of remediation decisions.  Participant consent and source confidentiality are necessary. These studies would provide evidence about whether the integrated interface improves review work rather than relying only on screenshots or developer impressions.  Figure 8.1: Proposed progression from reproducible benchmarks and broader coverage to controlled automation, deployment evaluation and user studies.   The roadmap can contain four stages:  Reconcile evidence and datasets.  Extend and evaluate analysis.  Validate deployment and automation.  Study developer outcomes.  Label the diagram “Proposed future work”. Do not include invented completion dates or percentage improvements.  REFERENCES [1] OWASP Foundation, “Static analysis,” OWASP Developer Guide. Available:  OWASP Static Analysis. [2] S. K. Basak, L. Neil, B. Reaves and L. Williams, “SecretBench: A Dataset of Software Secrets,” 2023, arXiv:2303.06729. Available:  SecretBench. [3] X. Zhou, S. Cao, X. Sun and D. Lo, “Large Language Model for Vulnerability Detection and Repair: Literature Review and the Road Ahead,” 2024, arXiv:2404.02525. Available:  Vulnerability Detection and Repair Review. [4] P. Lewis et al., “Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks,” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, vol. 33, 2020. Available:  Retrieval-Augmented Generation. [5] MITRE, “About CWE.” Available:  Common Weakness Enumeration. [6] FIRST.Org, “Common Vulnerability Scoring System v3.1: Specification Document,” 2019. Available:  CVSS v3.1 Specification. [7] Supabase, “Row Level Security,” Supabase Documentation. Available:  Row Level Security. APPENDICES APPENDIX A — PROJECT AND GROUP PHOTOGRAPHS [Insert genuine project and group photographs here.] Add a short caption identifying the activity, location and date where known. Obtain permission from identifiable participants. These photographs document project activity rather than detection accuracy. APPENDIX B — INDUSTRY PHOTOGRAPHS AND CERTIFICATES [Insert relevant industry-visit photographs and authentic certificates here, if applicable.] If no industry visit or certificate applies to the project, remove this appendix or state “Not applicable”, according to the institution’s format. APPENDIX C — PROJECT COMPETITION AND AWARD CERTIFICATES [Insert verified participation or award certificates here.] Identify the event and date. Clearly distinguish participation from an award. The front-matter list of publications, competitions and patents should use the same verified records.
